power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Traditional approaches probe cognition by aligning brain activity to external stimuli, yet many cognitive processes are not time-locked to such events.

Building on evidence that band-limited neural activity often occurs as transient bursts, we articulate the burst-related potentials (BRP) as a unifying terminology for an emerging family of analyses obtained by aligning unfiltered timedomain waveforms to frequency-domain landmarks.

We outline practical considerations and caveats for computing BRPs, distinguish descriptive alignment from mechanistic inference, and set out how burst-locked analyses can complement stimulus-locked ones in the study of internally generated cognition.
A major goal in neuroscience is to uncover patterns of brain activity that reflect specific cognitive functions.
This is challenging because task-relevant signals are embedded within large, unrelated neural activity.
For decades, neurophysiological studies have relied on averaging responses across trials that are time-locked to external task events.
This procedure can increase the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) if the task-related response is consistent and occurs at a fixed latency relative to the stimulus 1 .
Combined with both invasive and non-invasive electrophysiological recordings, this approach reveals stimulus-locked components known as event-related potentials (ERP).

These ERPs are characterised by positive and negative deflections, leading several models to propose that ERP-dynamics reflect a superposition of damped oscillations at certain frequency bands, originating from perturbations of neural networks consisting of extrinsic ('forward') and re-entrant ('backward') connections 2,3.
ERPs therefore offer a time-domain representation of responses that are consistent in both timing and phase across trials.

Spectral methods extend this by transforming signals into a time-frequency representation (TFR), which additionally captures changes in the power of ongoing activity that are reliable in the frequency domain even when their phase varies across trials 4 .
For nearly a century, electrophysiological studies have demonstrated relationships between activity in different frequency bands and a plethora of cognitive functions.
However, both ERPs and traditional TFRs remain constrained by their dependence on locking to stimuli or responses.

Whereas these methods have profoundly advanced our understanding of how the brain interacts with the external world, many cognitive phenomena, including internal decision-making processes and spontaneous thoughts and memories, are not time-locked to external events.
As a result, external-event-based analyses may miss, smear, or mischaracterize the neural dynamics underlying such internally driven processes.
To address this limitation, we propose using transient band-limited high-power events (bursts) as an endogenous temporal reference for aligning neural data (Figure 1).

text.text: Importantly, bursts provide well-defined temporal landmarks that are intrinsic to the neural signal itself.
Although they can be influenced by stimuli and behaviour, they are not fixed to externally imposed trial markers.
This shifts the temporal anchor and experimental perspective from stimulus-locked analyses to intrinsic brain dynamics.

In the bottom panel, the black line is raw LFP; the green line marks the burst duration; the grey line is an ideal cosine at the burst frequency (15 Hz), with a trough at time 0; red lines indicate cycle-based predicted LFP troughs, computed as multiples of cycles at 15 Hz (i.e., 66.67 ms); and blue lines indicate cycle-based LFP peaks.

text.text: A growing literature relates stimulus-locked features of bursts, such as rate, duration, and frequency span, to oscillatory dynamics and cognition.
Yet these approaches remain externally oriented.
Accordingly, we advocate incorporating burst-locked analyses into the neuroscientist's methodological repertoire.
Aligning neural data to landmarks within bursts offers a framework for examining the temporal structure of internally generated neural activity.

The broader logic of anchoring measurements to endogenous neural events rather than to external triggers builds on established precedents; for example, neural-event-triggered fMRI aligned haemodynamic measures to spontaneously detected neural events 24 , and aligning unfiltered waveforms to betaburst landmarks has been used to reveal structured waveform motifs and laminar-specific current flow 10, 13, 17, 25, 26 .

text.text: Following recent contributions 13, 26 , we refer to the alignment of time-domain waveforms to burst landmarks as "burst-related potentials" (BRP).

text.text: We introduce this term not to claim a fundamentally new analysis, but to provide a unifying vocabulary for this emerging family of methods.

Our aim is threefold: to consolidate this family of analyses under a common terminology, to provide practical guidance and explicit caveats for computing BRPs, and to articulate a research agenda for using bursts as intrinsic temporal anchors.
Whether cognition is, in general, temporally organised around bursts remains an open question, and the BRP framework is suggested as a tool to test this hypothesis.
Bursts are defined as brief high-power events within specific frequency bands and can be identified using several spectro-temporal methods, as recently reviewed in refs. 20, 27 .

text.text: When computing the BRP, important considerations apply: 1.
Bands and frequencies of interest: the electrophysiological spectrum divides into frequency bands, each defined by a characteristic range and proposed to support different cognitive processes.
The BRP should therefore be computed separately for each band.

Although canonical definitions such as delta (0.1-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-12 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), gamma (30-80 Hz) and ripples (80-250 Hz) are often used, inter-individual variability in spectral organisation can be substantial.
Recent findings 13 further show that the spectrum segregates into two categories: high-rhythmicity bands with sustained oscillations and lowrhythmicity bands dominated by short-lived bursts.

text.text: BRPs differ systematically between these 'sustained' and 'transient' bands (ref. 13 and Figure 3), and the same nominal frequency can fall into either category depending on the individual.

text.text: It is therefore advisable to define bands according to individual rhythmicity profiles, and compute and read the BRP differently in each category: in a high-rhythmicity band it approximates a quasi-stationary oscillation, warranting a longer window and a phase-based landmark; in a low-rhythmicity band it captures a rapidly damped oscillation, better summarised over a short window around a single amplitude-based landmark.

Filtering effect: band-pass filtering can impose apparent rhythmicity on aperiodic activity, and a substantial fraction of putative bursts may reflect fluctuations of the aperiodic background rather than genuine oscillations 30 ; detection should therefore control for the aperiodic spectrum, for example by parameterising it out or by benchmarking against phase-randomised or aperiodic-matched surrogate data.

text.text: Caveats and best practices 136 Because BRPs depend on a chain of analytical choices, results can vary substantially across 137 pipelines, and several caveats deserve emphasis.
138 Circularity and the aperiodic background.

Detecting bursts within a narrow band and then 139 aligning to a landmark within that band can, by construction, return a band-limited, oscillatory-140 looking average even in the absence of a genuine oscillation, for instance when the procedure is applied to filtered aperiodic ('1/f') activity.

Guarding against this circularity requires (i) detecting bursts against an explicitly modelled aperiodic background 15, 30 , (ii) computing and validating the BRP on the raw signal rather than the filtered one, and (iii) benchmarking the observed waveform against phase-randomised or aperiodic-matched surrogate data.
text.formatted: Guarding against this circularity requires (i) detecting bursts against an explicitly modelled aperiodic background <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> , (ii) computing and validating the BRP on the raw signal rather than the filtered one, and (iii) benchmarking the observed waveform against phase-randomised or aperiodic-matched surrogate data.

text.text: Convergent, non-circular evidence including concurrent spiking, laminar current-source density, or independent behavioural correlates can provide stronger support that a BRP reflects a physiological event.
Reproducibility.
The burst-detection algorithm, spectral-decomposition method, thresholding criterion, treatment of overlapping bursts, and band definitions each shape the resulting BRP 27, 28 .

text.text: Aligning waveforms to bursts is a descriptive operation; on its own it does not license claims about the generating circuit.

Burst waveforms are nonetheless not arbitrary: the extracellular field is believed to originate from largescale synchronous synaptic activity 35 , and biophysical modelling and laminar recordings indicate that beta-burst shape reflects the timing and strength of synaptic inputs targeting different cortical layers, with deep-and superficial-layer currents flowing in opposite directions 10, 25 .
text.formatted: Burst waveforms are nonetheless not arbitrary: the extracellular field is believed to originate from largescale synchronous synaptic activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> , and biophysical modelling and laminar recordings indicate that beta-burst shape reflects the timing and strength of synaptic inputs targeting different cortical layers, with deep-and superficial-layer currents flowing in opposite directions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: BRPs can thus serve as a bridge to mechanistic models, but mechanistic interpretation requires additional, layeror circuit-resolved evidence.
BRPs provide a low-dimensional, physiologically grounded, easy-to-visualize signature of neural events.
While prior work has focused on beta and gamma bursts, BRPs generalise to bursts in any frequency.

By serving as a brain-internal temporal reference, BRPs complement event-locked analyses, capturing the dynamics of internal neural events in ways that are largely inaccessible to traditional measures, as illustrated below.

Waveform-based characterization of neural events: anchoring unfiltered waveforms to physiologically meaningful time points enables classification of bursts based on waveform shape, offering access to functional variability beyond averaging.

Although the average burst waveform appears conserved across studies, subjects, and species 17 , individual bursts exhibit diverse temporal dynamics that are not captured by standard time-frequency methods 27, 31 (Figure 3B).

text.text: From a physiological perspective, differences in waveform morphology arise from variability in synaptic inputs 17 and the engagement of distinct cell assemblies 9, 22 .

text.text: These differences in turn support functional specialization, as recent studies associate specific waveform motifs with particular task demands 25 .
text.formatted: These differences in turn support functional specialization, as recent studies associate specific waveform motifs with particular task demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: BRPs therefore provide an anchor for classifying burst waveforms into motifs, yielding a rich source of information about their mechanisms and functional roles.
the BRP, or subsets of BRPs defined by waveform motifs, can be convolved with raw signals to identify time points that resemble BRP-like activation.

This approach has recently been used to improve performance in movement-imagery braincomputer interfaces (BCI) 36 , demonstrating that task-related changes in burst waveform shape carry informative signals at the single-trial level.

text.text: More generally, BRPs or their motifs can be viewed as tailored filters that allow estimation of the degree of activation of subthreshold activity.
After BRP extraction, cognitively relevant bursts that do not exceed conventional detection thresholds may therefore become detectable.

defining events based on physiologically meaningful landmarks allows investigation of both induced and spontaneous, stimulus-free events, such as activity during rest or waiting periods within a task.

This creates a bridge between the extensive literature on anatomical networks showing correlated activity (restingstate networks 37 ) and the sub-second activation of networks within and across specific frequency bands 38, 39 .

text.text: This logic is well established in sleep research, where aligning to endogenous slow oscillations, spindles and ripples is routinely done, and has illuminated memory consolidation 40 , and it has recently been extended to waking cortico-muscular interactions by realigning MEG to bursts, revealing transient connectivity that trial-averaging obscures 41 .

text.text: Because bursts also propagate as spatiotemporal (travelling-wave) patterns with distinct behavioural correlates 28 , burst landmarks additionally provide a reference for studying the spatial spread and long-range coordination of internally generated events.

text.text: Moreover, computing task-specific BRPs-for example, those aligned to the first burst following a stimulus-enables direct linking of network activation to specific cognitive functions.
an analysis that focuses on the brain-derived signal essentially removes any temporal jitter that typically infests time-locked analyses to external (e.g., task-related) events.
As a result the BRP's signal-to-noise ratio is improved.
This benefit is expected to be more pronounced higher in the processing hierarchy, due to accumulation of response variability 42, 43 .

text.text: The comparable magnitudes of BRPs and ERPs (Figure 3C) are therefore encouraging, especially given that BRPs are aligned to internal events rather than to salient external triggers that impose strong synchronization.

text.text: As a result, BRPs may substantially enhance SNR and reveal consistent neural patterns associated with internal cognitive events that are blurred or lost in conventional ERP analyses.
Temporal anchoring matters.
Traditional ERPs and TFRs reveal how the brain responds to external events but overlook the dynamics of internally generated cognition.
By treating bursts as natural temporal anchors, BRPs complement these approaches and provide access to the temporal dynamics of endogenous events.
The signal-processing tools required for BRP computation are readily available on standard computers and implemented in freely accessible software packages.

As adoption grows, standardized pipelines for burst detection, visualization, analysis, and interpretation can be developed, improving comparability across studies, modalities, and species, and opening a window onto the fundamental building blocks of cognition as those spontaneously occur.
At the neural level, these building blocks are commonly understood as activations of neuronal cell assemblies, and a key promise of BRPs is to help access them non-invasively.

According to the cell assembly framework 44 , neurons that are repeatedly co-activated form functional ensembles whose activations unfold as packets of sequential neuronal activity 45 , and whose synchronous synaptic processing can leave spectral fingerprints detectable as bursts in local field potentials (LFP) 46 .

text.text: Consistent with this view, burst-locked firing rates track LFP peaks and troughs 9, 22 (although, as noted above, this correspondence is not always trivial 23 ), underscoring the BRPs to illuminate neural computation and communication.

text.text: In sum, BRPs provide a complementary route to neural processes as those occur.

They support waveform-based characterization of neural events, single-trial analysis and decoding, event-based analyses beyond stimulus locking, and improved signal-to-noise through reduced temporal jitter.

Most importantly, by linking internally driven cognitive processes with external events and behaviour, BRPs shift the temporal reference frame from externally imposed timing to the brain's intrinsic dynamics, offering a window into cognition at "its own time".

A. Continuous activity contains transient bursts (shaded), driven either by external stimuli (left, orange; arrows mark stimulus times) or by internally generated events such as spontaneous thoughts (right, blue; arrows mark internal events).

B. Alignment schemes.
